title: Using Adjectives as Nouns
goal: Use Norwegian adjectives as noun phrases with correct definiteness, number, and neuter forms.

objectives.statement: Use Norwegian adjectives as noun phrases with correct definiteness, number, and neuter forms.

spans.value: Maja and Erik are furnishing a small apartment. They have found several possible tables, chairs, lamps, and cupboards, but they cannot take everything.
Hvilket bord skal vi kjøpe?
Det lille passer best på kjøkkenet.

blocks.translation: The small one fits best in the kitchen.

spans.value: Hva med stolene?
Vi tar de blå, ikke de svarte.

blocks.translation: We’ll take the blue ones, not the black ones.

spans.value: Trenger vi også et skap?

blocks.translation: Do we also need a cupboard?

spans.value: Ja, men ikke det høye. Jeg liker det lave.

blocks.translation: Yes, but not the tall one. I like the low one.

spans.value: Og lampene? Den gamle er fin.

blocks.translation: And the lamps? The old one is nice.

spans.value: Den er fin, men vi trenger en ny.

blocks.translation: It is nice, but we need a new one.

spans.value: Maja and Erik repeatedly leave out nouns that are already clear from the conversation. Instead of saying det lille bordet, Erik says det lille. Instead of repeating de blå stolene, he says de blå.

Norwegian can therefore use an adjective as a complete noun phrase. The adjective describes an understood person or thing. Context identifies the omitted noun, while determiners and adjective agreement jointly express relevant features such as number, definiteness, and, in singular forms, gender where the forms distinguish them.
The usual Norwegian term is a nominalized adjective (substantivert adjektiv).

This is similar to English expressions such as the blue one and the old ones. Norwegian does not normally add a word corresponding to one or ones. The adjective takes the agreement form required by the understood noun, although some forms are identical and do not overtly reveal every feature.

sections.title: Understanding what has been left out

spans.value: Look at Erik’s first answer:

no.value: Det lille passer best på kjøkkenet.

en.value: The small one fits best in the kitchen.

Identify-the-understood-noun

This noticing activity belongs here because the learner must first connect each adjective phrase to something already present in the context. Use Maja and Erik’s shop conversation. For each shortened phrase, the learner should state which previously mentioned object is understood. Success demonstrates that the learner recognizes why the noun can be omitted; adjective endings are not yet the primary scored goal.

sections.title: Definite forms: the red one and the red ones

spans.value: A definite phrase points to a particular person or thing: the small one, the old one, the blue ones. Norwegian normally uses den, det, or de before a definite adjective used without a noun.
Common-gender singular:
Neuter singular:
Plural:
The adjective usually has the definite ending -e in all three patterns.
The understood noun might be en stol, en kopp, or another common-gender noun.
Here the understood noun is neuter, perhaps et skjerf or et glass.
Here more than one item is understood.
The compact rule is:

statement.value: For a definite adjective phrase without a noun, choose den, det, or de from the gender and number of the understood noun, and normally use the adjective’s -e form.

spans.value: This means that neuter singular has det, but the adjective does not keep its indefinite neuter -t ending.

Distinguish-definite-gender-and-number

This controlled recognition activity uses objects in the second-hand shop. The learner should identify whether each definite adjective phrase refers to one common-gender object, one neuter object, or several objects. Success demonstrates correct interpretation of den, det, and de. Adjective meaning serves only as context.

She wants to buy the large one.

spans.value: The first sentence in each pair introduces an unspecified item. The second points to a particular item that the speakers can identify.
Another common mistake is to use the English word one as if Norwegian required an extra noun:
This form can occur in informal speech in some contexts, but it is not the basic pattern taught here. The standard, economical phrase is:
Contrast-indefinite-and-definite-singular

This activity uses Maja and Erik before and after they have chosen particular items. The learner should complete short exchanges with an adjective phrase that either introduces an unspecified object or identifies a particular known object. Success demonstrates the definiteness contrast between en/et plus the indefinite adjective and den/det plus the definite adjective. Number remains singular throughout.

sections.title: Plural forms: new ones and the new ones

spans.value: When several items are meant, the adjective takes its plural form. An indefinite plural adjective phrase often has no article:
When the plural group is definite, use de:

en.value: We are buying the new ones.
The cheap ones are by the door.

spans.value: Compare:

en.value: Erik is looking for old lamps.
Erik is looking for old ones.

no.value: Erik ser etter de gamle lampene.

en.value: Erik is looking for the old lamps.
Erik is looking for the old ones.

spans.value: In the indefinite plural, gamle appears without de. In the definite plural, de gamle refers to a particular known group.
Do not automatically use de merely because the meaning is plural. The choice depends on definiteness:
The black items have not yet been identified.
The speakers are choosing a particular visible group.
Separate-plural-number-from-definiteness

This sorting activity belongs here because learners may wrongly treat de as a general plural marker. Use shop statements about searching for items and selecting visible items. The learner should decide whether each context requires an indefinite plural adjective or a definite plural phrase with de. Success demonstrates the definiteness decision within plural noun phrases; adjective spelling is supplied as context rather than scored.
The dialogue uses:
The adjective liten follows forms that learners may already know from adjective agreement:
Common-gender singular:
Neuter singular:
Plural:
The adjective is still agreeing with an understood noun. Omitting the noun does not make liten regular.
Retrieve-forms-of-liten

This focused activity uses the table, lamp, and chairs from the original scene. The learner should replace full phrases containing liten with adjective-only noun phrases. Success demonstrates retention of liten, lite, lille, and små according to definiteness, gender, and number.
After walking around the shop, Maja and Erik compare their final choices.
Vi kan ikke kjøpe begge bordene. Tar vi det store eller det lille?

blocks.translation: We can’t buy both tables. Are we taking the large one or the small one?

spans.value: Vi tar det lille. Men vi trenger store stoler.

blocks.translation: We’ll take the small one. But we need large chairs.

spans.value: De store ved vinduet er fine.

blocks.translation: The large ones by the window are nice.

spans.value: Ja, men de er dyre. Finnes det andre stoler?

blocks.translation: Yes, but they are expensive. Are there other chairs?

spans.value: Ja, jeg så noen svarte ved døra.

blocks.translation: Yes, I saw some black ones by the door.

spans.value: Jeg liker ikke de svarte. La oss ta de blå.

blocks.translation: I don’t like the black ones. Let’s take the blue ones.

spans.value: Notice how the same adjective can appear in different phrases as the situation changes:
The items are plural but not yet identified.

no.value: De store ved vinduet er fine.

en.value: The large ones by the window are nice.

spans.value: The speakers now mean a particular group.
Likewise:
This introduces an indefinite group.

en.value: I don’t like the black ones.

spans.value: This refers back to that known group.
The essential decision is not whether the noun is spoken aloud. The essential decision is what the understood noun phrase means:

items.value: If singular, is the understood noun common gender or neuter?
Is the person or thing indefinite or definite?
Which adjective form agrees with those features?

spans.value: Track-reference-across-the-dialogue

This contextual activity uses the second conversation. The learner should follow how an indefinite adjective phrase introduces a group and how a later definite phrase refers back to it. Success demonstrates control of definiteness across connected turns rather than in isolated sentences. Number and adjective agreement remain necessary context, but reference tracking is the primary scored goal.

At a bakery, Nora and Hassan are choosing cakes for a meeting. Several cakes are already on the counter, so both speakers can see which ones they mean. Some cake names use common-gender nouns, while others use neuter nouns.

The learner should first describe an unspecified choice, such as wanting a small one or needing two large ones. Next, the learner should identify a particular visible choice, such as choosing the small one or rejecting the expensive ones. The nouns should then be omitted once the context makes them clear.
Transfer-adjective-noun-phrases-to-the-bakery

This cumulative activity changes the setting while preserving the target grammar. The learner should produce short Norwegian responses using adjectives as complete noun phrases for indefinite and definite choices, singular common-gender and neuter items, and plural items. Success demonstrates coordinated control of definiteness, number, and neuter forms without relying on wording from the furniture-shop dialogue.
Recall-the-core-patterns

Without looking back, the learner should give Norwegian phrases for an indefinite common-gender one, an indefinite neuter one, a definite common-gender one, a definite neuter one, indefinite plural ones, and definite plural ones, using one familiar adjective. Success demonstrates retrieval of the complete agreement pattern for adjectives used as noun phrases.

prompt.value: A shop assistant has mentioned «et lite bord» and «de blå stolene». Later, the assistant refers to them only as «det lille» and «de blå». Choose the complete interpretation for both shortened phrases. Focus on which nouns are understood; adjective endings are not the primary target.

options.text: det lille viser til stolene; de blå viser til et bord
det lille viser til et bord; de blå viser til stolene
options.why: The shop context makes et bord the understood noun for det lille and stolene the understood plural noun for de blå.

options.text: det lille viser til et skjerf; de blå viser til en stol
options.why: These references do not match the established shop context or the singular and plural phrases.

prompt.value: Read this shop exchange: «Vi trenger noen svarte stoler. De svarte står ved døra, og de blå står ved vinduet.» Choose the complete interpretation showing which phrase introduces an indefinite group, which phrase refers back to it, and which phrase identifies the other known group.

options.text: noen svarte og de svarte viser begge til en kjent gruppe; de blå introduserer en ny gruppe
options.why: Noen is indefinite, and de does not introduce an indefinite group.

options.text: noen svarte introduserer en gruppe; de svarte viser til en annen gruppe; de blå viser tilbake til de svarte
options.why: The later phrase de svarte is the one that refers back to the introduced group.

options.text: noen svarte introduserer noen svarte stoler; de svarte viser tilbake til disse stolene; de blå viser til en annen kjent gruppe blå stoler
options.why: Noen introduces an indefinite group, de svarte refers back to that group, and de blå identifies another known group.

stem.value: Which interpretation correctly tracks noen svarte, de svarte, and de blå?

prompt.value: At a bakery, Nora and Hassan are choosing cakes for a meeting. Write six short Norwegian responses using adjectives as complete noun phrases and omitting the cake nouns. Cover these situations: an unspecified singular common-gender cake, an unspecified singular neuter cake, a particular visible common-gender cake, a particular visible neuter cake, an unspecified plural group, and a particular visible plural group. Use familiar adjectives from the lesson, but create bakery responses rather than copying a complete furniture-shop sentence.

payload.judge_prompt: Check all six requested bakery responses and report evidence for each criterion. Accept any adjective form taught in the lesson when it agrees with the requested definiteness, gender, and number; do not require one particular adjective. Each response must use an adjective-only noun phrase rather than speaking the cake noun.

criteria.instruction: Includes an unspecified singular common-gender bakery choice with en and an agreeing adjective form.
Includes an unspecified singular neuter bakery choice with et and an agreeing adjective form.
Includes a particular singular common-gender bakery choice with den and a definite adjective form.
Includes a particular singular neuter bakery choice with det and a definite adjective form.
Includes an unspecified plural bakery choice with the plural adjective form and no de.
Includes a particular plural bakery choice with de and the plural adjective form.
